extracted.intended_audience: NeurIPS authors, reviewers, conference organizers, and researchers interested in LLMs for peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and using an LLM-based Checklist Assistant to vet conference paper submissions against a conference's paper checklist, aimed at helping authors ensure compliance and improve papers (not replacing human reviewers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors felt the Checklist Assistant was a valuable enhancement to the paper submission process. The majority (>70%) of surveyed authors reported a positive experience using the LLM Checklist Assistant and >70% said they would modify their paper in response to feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess via pre- and post-usage surveys (expect possible drop in positivity after actual use). Metrics: percent reporting usefulness, percent reporting intent to modify, qualitative feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to help authors improve submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: When authors submitted to the Checklist Assistant multiple times they almost always made changes to their checklists between submissions and significantly lengthened their answers, suggesting they may have added content in response to LLM feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure changes in checklist answers/justifications across submissions (e.g., answer flips like 'NA'→'Yes', counts of changed justifications, multiplicative increase in word count). Note: observed changes are suggestive but not necessarily causal evidence that the assistant caused paper improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Inaccuracy was one of the most frequently cited problems by authors (20/52 respondents). The deployment exhibited accuracy issues and alignment problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track and report factual correctness and false positives/negatives in assistant outputs; accuracy failures undermine utility and can mislead authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too strict in requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors reported that the LLM was 'too strict in its requirements' (14/52 respondents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor whether the assistant imposes overly stringent interpretations of checklist questions or marks acceptable content as deficient; calibrate strictness to intended checklist semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete, grounded feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The LLM was able to give concrete feedback to authors grounded in the content of their paper and checklist. It was capable of giving concrete and specific feedback for many questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer outputs that cite or point to specific evidence in the paper and give actionable suggestions; measure how often feedback is paper-grounded vs generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to produce generic boilerplate
rubrics_metrics.description: The LLM tended to provide some generic boilerplate as part of its responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect boilerplate by repetition, vagueness, or lack of linkage to the paper; encourage specificity and limit templated language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope expansion beyond checklist questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The assistant sometimes 'expand[ed] the scope of questions' beyond what was asked in the checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the assistant sticks to the checklist's intended scope; evaluate whether scope expansion is helpful or introduces irrelevant demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback granularity / verbosity (points per question)
rubrics_metrics.description: The LLM tended to provide 4–6 distinct and specific points of feedback per question across the 15 checklist questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect multi-point feedback; monitor verbosity and whether number of points is useful vs overwhelming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to gaming / adversarial manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors could adversarially improve their chance of passing an automated LLM Checklist review by modifying their checklist without modifying their paper: an automated attack increased scores on 14 out of 15 questions. The attacker LLM used illegitimate strategies (e.g., adding hardware descriptions not present in the paper, fabricating a code repository URL) that were accepted by the Checklist Assistant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test robustness with adversarial attack simulations; do not deploy LLM verification as an automated gate without defenses against fabricated or misleading justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended use: aid authors, not automated verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The intended use of our Checklist Assistant was to help authors improve their papers, not to serve as a tool for reviewers to verify the accuracy of authors’ responses. Using it as automated verification creates incentives for gaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design policy and deployment so outputs are shown only to authors and not used as a substitute for human verification unless robustness is proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation against replacing human review
rubrics_metrics.description: An LLM Checklist Assistant can effectively aid authors in ensuring scientific rigor, but should likely not be used as a fully automated review tool that replaces human review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an author-facing assistant; continue to rely on human reviewers for evaluation and verification of submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for improved robustness and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The study points to notable limitations that need to be addressed, in particular accuracy and alignment issues. The system was not robust to gaming, suggesting limitations for deployment in the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize work on alignment, factuality, and anti-gaming defenses before broader or enforcement-oriented deployment. Monitor failure modes and iterate.
